title: Should Students Raise Their Hand In Small Groups? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/02/14/should-students-raise-their-hand-in-small-groups/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: While affirming that hand-raising is good practice for whole-class instruction, Michael Linsin argues teachers should abandon the requirement during small-group work of four or five students. He lists five reasons: it dampens the natural energy and spontaneity of discussion, discourages active peer-to-peer participation, increases self-consciousness in the already-intimate small-group setting, poorly prepares students for eventually running their own discussions without a teacher present, and takes the enjoyment out of leading groups for the teacher. Linsin recommends instead modeling productive small-group conversation skills in detail beforehand—eye contact, polite questioning, chiming in without interrupting—and then allowing free-flowing discussion, with the teacher acting as a facilitator who gradually recedes into the background.
points: Hand-raising is affirmed as good practice for whole-class instruction but is argued to be counterproductive in small groups of four or five students.
Reasons cited include dampened spontaneity, discouraged peer-to-peer participation, increased self-consciousness, and poor preparation for students eventually leading their own discussions.
Requiring hand-raising in small groups is also described as reducing the teacher's own enjoyment of facilitating group discussion.
The recommended approach is to model productive conversation skills in detail beforehand—eye contact, polite questioning, chiming in without interrupting.
The teacher's long-term role in small groups should be to gradually recede into the background as a facilitator rather than a moderator of every turn.
quotes: Requiring students to raise their hand before speaking is good classroom management practice.
The truth is, with groups this size, it’s best to shelve the practice.
Asking students to raise their hand takes the joy out of being in a small group. It removes the essence, the seasoning, the élan of debate and discussion.
Your students must be able to speak directly to fellow group members without going through you first. Otherwise, they’ll grow bored with the process.
Another important goal should be to become less and less involved, to raise questions or advance ideas and then fade into the background.
Before jumping into small groups it’s important to model in detail what productive conversation looks like, including how to make eye contact, ask polite questions, and chime in without interrupting.
